items.abstract: Contrary to what is suggested by the chapter’s heading, ‘Validity’, PECL ch 4 does not deal with all the requirements for a contract’s validity but has a rather limited scope of application. This scope is defined negatively by Art 4:101, which excludes invalidity arising from illegality, immorality, and lack of capacity.

items.abstract: <jats:p>Related-party transactions are ubiquitous in corporate life. They are neither inherently benign nor inherently abusive: used properly, they can reduce transaction costs, stabilize supply and value chains, and create commercial opportunities; abused by controlling shareholders, actual controllers, directors, supervisors, senior executives, or their affiliates, they can become channels for tunneling, self-dealing, and the diversion of corporate wealth. China’s 2023 Company Law responds through a cluster of rules rather than a single provision. This article argues that those rules should be read systemically around three core principles: procedural rigor, information transparency, and fair consideration. A lawful related-party transaction should satisfy all three. The article then develops a threefold remedial framework under company law, tort law, and contract law. Company-law remedies include judicial review of defective shareholder or board resolutions, derivative litigation, and the corporate right of disgorgement. Securities law supplements this framework for listed companies through disclosure liability. From a tort-law perspective, Article 22 of the 2023 Company Law should be understood as creating a special, objective form of liability for abusive related-party transactions rather than ordinary fault-based tort liability. From a contract-law perspective, Article 22 should also be treated as a validity-affecting mandatory rule capable of supporting invalidity where a related-party transaction abuses a relationship and harms the company. Disgorgement and compensatory damages should operate cumulatively or in the alternative according to the relationship between the fiduciary’s improper gain and the company’s loss. The article further argues that company charters and supplementary labor- and civillaw rules should prevent mid-level managers from exploiting gaps in the statutory definition of senior management. The broader aim is neither to prohibit related-party transactions nor to indulge them, but to channel them toward marketization, transparency, fairness, and rational corporate governance. The law should preserve beneficial transactions while providing effective, low-cost remedies against transactions that transfer value out of the company.</jats:p>
title: Regulating Related-Party Transactions in China: A Threefold Analysis under Company Law, Tort Law, and Contract Law

items.abstract: The economic relevance of agency is an often-invoked truism. Indeed, today’s business world could not operate without the possibility of contracts being negotiated, concluded, and performed by persons not designated to become a party to them. In an economy based on the division of labour, principals do not harness intermediaries just for their skills, knowledge, reputation, and to surmount geographical distance.

items.abstract: <jats:p><span>For decades, common law contract interpretation has been defined by a contextualist turn, where the search for commercial common sense routinely bypassed the Parol Evidence Rule. This article contends that we are witnessing an inadvertent mutation — not resurrection — of the Rule: not as a revived judicial doctrine, but as a structural sealant. Through four distinct mechanisms — procedural, record, execution, and governance — digital infrastructures now privilege textually fixed, machine-executable meaning over open-textured interpretation. The result is the Silicon Seal: a structural tendency toward contractual finality that operates alongside, and sometimes more powerfully than, traditional evidentiary limits. Drawing on comparative common law materials from England, Singapore, and the United States, the article reconstitutes the court's role as auditor of automated performance and poses four normative questions that contract law has not yet thought to ask.</span></jats:p>
title: THE SILICON SEAL: Algorithms and the Finality of Contract

items.abstract: <jats:p> The Privy Council in East Asia Company Ltd v PT Satria Tirtatama Energindo (a case on appeal from Bermuda) has provided clarification on the correct approach to the reliance aspect of apparent authority. Reliance can be of particular importance where the third party has been put on notice as to the agent’s lack of authority: for example, when the transaction is unusual or especially onerous for the principal. The Privy Council concluded, albeit obiter, that the correct test is one of reasonable reliance by the third party. In doing so, it has rejected the approach adopted by Lord Neuberger NPJ in the Hong Kong case of Akai Holdings and subsequently followed in a number of English decisions: that is, reliance by the third party is presumed in the absence of dishonesty or irrationality. </jats:p>
title: Reasonable Reliance and Apparent Authority: East Asia Company Ltd v PT Satria Tirtatama Energindo [2019] UKPC 30
